How to lose weight with Hashimoto's disease?

This. Even on people who have no disease besides being overweight or obese, eating less is the key to losing weight, no matter how much exercise you do. Still, I'd try to find a way to exercise, just for your health.
I am eating as little as possible. With this and hormones my weight is slowly decreasing, about a kg/two weeks.

That's really how you want to lose weight: slowly. If it's going down that's great. If you're not counting calories/macronutrients you may be eating more than you think and in the wrong proportions (usually more carbs than proteins and fats).

Future PT here. What you described is basically the jist of exercise; it sucks until your body adapts to it. The more you do it the less it hurts and more weight you will lose. Walking is one of the best things you can do for exercise, but if it it hurting too much on your joints try using an elliptical machine or a swimming routine. However those should not replace walking, it should supplement it; you need weight bearing on your joints in order for them to get better.

In addition to exercise, moving to a plant based diet will help out tremendously. Its hard to eat too many calories when all you eat is unrefined plants foods. Additionally, (this is out of my scope of field so take it with a grain a salt) there is some research on gut bacteria that love meats and dairy that increase inflammation. Feed yourself plants and good bacteria that is less inflammatory will grow in your gut leading to less fat storage.

Edit: Glad you're looking for help. If it's hard make an appointment with a physical therapist for training. They will know whats right for you more than a personal trainer, especially if you find one with a doctorate degree. Good luck!
Ehh, it sucks that I can't really afford anything you mentioned. Looks like more walking and eating vegan it is.

You don't need to eat vegan. You need to severely reduce your simple carbohydrate intake. From what I hear anything high on the glycemic index (simple carbs) kick Hashimoto's into high gear. Greens and such are great for you, but you don't need to go without proteins. Proteins and veggies will fill you up quicker than you'd think. Have you thought about Keto or Paleo? (Not a keto/paleo nut, just think it might be ideal in your situation.)

Fake sugar - results may vary depending on the type for you. Try them out, figure out what's palatable and what still triggers your thyroid. Some of them will and some of them won't. Find out what works for you.

Find a pool and swim if you can. It will suck and suck hard at first, but it will get better over time. Your endurance will go up. And yes, walk some as well. Gradually over time it will get better and your joints will adjust.

I know you're being sarcastic, but I haven't done much reading about starvation mode. I always assumed it was when your body starts eating the fat excessively more than normal, since it isn't getting the calories it needs. Is this not the case? I'm totally serious.

It's basically when your body isn't getting enough calories so it slows down your metabolism to use as little energy as possible. All the fatties think that not eating for two hours puts you in starvation mode and makes you gain 100lbs.

I can confirm the two-hour thing. The ones at my work basically have kitchens for desks and are always snacking on a candy bar or potato chips. I'm not sure I know what starvation mode feels like, but I can go til 5:00 without eating before feeling like I reaaaally need some food. I don't do it often, but there is a day every now and then when I spend my lunch running errands rather than eating.

The myth of starvation mode originated, like all stupid things, largely thanks to misinterpreting a scientific study. People twisted the fact that participants had a significant drop in metabolic rate (after 24 weeks of significantly reduced diet) as their body adapting to the fewer calories, but it was largely simply because they had a lower mass and thus needed to burn fewer calories.

This got confounded with the real phenomenon of animal starvation response, which reduces the metabolic rate during low calorie times. It's takes days to have any significant effect and, while your body does try to restore the stored energy levels it lost it's not going to make someone obese, and if you keep a calorie balance or deficit you will not gain weight (obviously.)

Additionally, people who are trying to lose weight are likely to underestimate their calorie consumption, overestimate their calorie expenditures, and gain muscle.

Diets need to be referred solely as how you eat all the time, rather than something you do every now and then to feel good about yourself.
